title: The Grief Support Group Facilitator's Handbook
summary: A working handbook for running a grief support group: the session arc, what surfaces week by week, anniversaries, comparing losses, and closing the group well.
body_markdown:
Setting a grief group up is one job. Running it week after week is a different one, and it is the part nobody hands you a document for. You have a purpose statement, a schedule and eight people, and then session three arrives and someone says their sister's birthday is on Thursday and the room goes quiet.


This handbook for grief support group facilitators is about that part. It assumes the group already exists. If you are still deciding what kind of group to run and who it is for, start with[How to Start a Grief Support Group](https://www.mentalhappy.com/blog/how-to-start-a-grief-support-group) . If you want the scope and safety material, that is in[Support Group Boundaries: Scope and Safety](https://www.mentalhappy.com/blog/support-group-boundaries-scope-and-safety) .


## The short version


- Give every session the same shape. Predictability is what lets people take risks inside it.
- Do not run the group on a stage model of grief. Grief oscillates rather than progresses.
- The feelings members apologize for, relief, anger, numbness, are usually the ones worth the most room.
- Track the dates. Anniversaries, birthdays and holidays will do more to your group calendar than any topic you plan.
- Never end on the heaviest thing said. Protect the last eight minutes.
- Plan the ending of the group from the beginning, especially in a closed cohort.


## How to structure a grief support group session


In a grief group the structure is not administration, it is containment. Members are managing something unpredictable all week. An hour that runs the same way each time is an hour they do not have to brace for.


A workable 60 minute arc:


Minutes What is happening Why it is there


0 to 5 Welcome, name the topic, one line on how the hour will run Tells people what they are walking into


5 to 15 Check in, one contained question, passing allowed Takes the temperature without opening the deepest thing first


15 to 22 A short piece of psychoeducation or a framing thought Gives the discussion something to push against


22 to 45 The main discussion The reason they came


45 to 52 Reflection or a short exercise Moves people from talking to noticing


52 to 60 Integration and a deliberate close Brings everyone back into the room


For 90 minutes, stretch the discussion and the reflection, not the check-in. A check-in that runs long is the single most common way a grief session loses its second half.


**The timings are a shape, not a schedule. What matters is that the last eight minutes exist and that you protect them.**


## Session one: setting the floor


Do not open with "tell us about your loss." For most people that is far too much in a room of strangers, and it teaches the group that depth is the price of admission.


Cover, in this order: what the group is and is not, how the hour runs, the agreements, what confidentiality means and where it stops, and that nobody is required to share. Then ask something people can answer at any depth they choose.


- "What made you decide to come?"
- "What would make this hour useful to you?"
- "If you want to, one word for how you're arriving today."


The first session succeeds if people come back. It does not need to contain anyone's whole story.


## What tends to surface, and roughly when


This is a pattern, not a rule, and any group can run it out of order. It is useful mostly so you are not caught flat.


- **Early sessions.** The facts. What happened, the hospital, the phone call, the funeral, who behaved badly. People need the account heard before they can move off it.
- **Once the group settles.** The secondary losses. The house, the income, the friendships that fell away, the role they no longer have, the future they had assumed.
- **Mid group.** The material people were embarrassed to start with. Relief. Anger. The things they said or did not say. Guilt about a good day.
- **Later.** Identity. Who they are now. What to do with the relationship going forward rather than how to end it.


If your plan says week four is about coping strategies and the group is somewhere else entirely, follow the group. The plan exists to stop you drifting, not to override what is in the room.


## Do not run the group on stages


Members arrive expecting grief to have a sequence, and the stage language is everywhere. It causes real harm in a group, because someone who is angry in week seven concludes they have gone backward.


A more useful frame to hold, and to offer members, is the dual process model described by Stroebe and Schut, in which bereaved people move back and forth between confronting the loss and getting on with a changed life. The oscillation is the process. Not the arrival at a stage.


In practice that means a member who spent last week crying and this week talking about a job application has not skipped anything or shut down. It also means you do not need to steer anyone toward a mood.


**A phrase worth having: "Grief tends to move back and forth rather than forward. A good week doesn't undo a hard one, and a hard one doesn't cancel the good week."**


## When members compare losses


This will happen. Someone says "but mine isn't as bad as yours," or "at least she lived a long life," or a member who lost a parent goes quiet after a member who lost a child speaks.


Left alone, comparison quietly sorts the group into people who have earned their grief and people who have not, and the second group stops talking.


Name it early and name it as a group agreement rather than a correction of one person:


- "We don't rank losses here. What you're carrying is what you're carrying."
- "You don't need to qualify it before you say it."
- "I've noticed a few people apologizing before they share. You don't have to earn the space."


If someone persistently minimizes their own loss, that is worth a gentle private word, not a public one.


## Tears, silence and laughter


All three worry new facilitators and none of them is a problem.


**Tears.** Let them happen. Do not rush in with tissues and reassurance, which reads as "please stop." "Take your time" and "you don't need to apologize" are usually enough. Stay attentive to whether the person is moving past what the group can hold, which is a different thing from crying.


**Silence.** After a hard disclosure, silence is often the group doing its job. Count to ten before you fill it. If you always fill it, you teach the group that silence is an emergency.


**Laughter.** Grief groups laugh, sometimes hard, often about the person who died. It is not avoidance and it is not disrespect. Let it run. The one time to look closer is laughter that seems to be covering something, and even then you notice rather than name it in front of everyone.


## The feelings members apologize for


The most valuable material in a grief group is usually prefaced with "this is going to sound awful."


- **Relief.** Especially after a long illness or a difficult relationship. Members often believe it disqualifies their grief. It does not, and saying so plainly can be the most useful sentence of the session.
- **Anger at the person who died.** For the debts, the secrets, the not going to the doctor, the leaving. Very hard to say out loud and very common.
- **Numbness.** "I haven't cried once." Members read this as evidence they did not love the person enough.
- **Guilt about an ordinary day.** Enjoying something, and then the drop.


You do not need to interpret any of it. What helps is making clear that the group is a place where these can be said without being explained away.


"That's a common thing to feel and a hard thing to say. Thank you for saying it" does more work than analysis.


## Anniversaries and holidays will run your calendar


Anniversaries, birthdays, the date of the diagnosis, the last holiday together, the wedding anniversary, the day the house sold. These arrive whether or not your session plan has room for them.


- Ask early, and once, whether anyone has dates coming up in the life of the group. Keep a private note. Do not announce them.
- In the session before a member's date, leave space for it without putting them on the spot. "I know this week has something in it for one or two people. If you want the room, it's here."
- Expect the run-up to be harder than the day itself for many people. The day often arrives already braced for.
- Do not let the group manufacture a ritual on someone's behalf unless they have asked for one.


**Holidays.** The first round of them is its own event. A dedicated session before the season, covering what members are dreading, what they are being asked to attend, what they are allowed to decline, and what they want to do with the empty chair, tends to be one of the most used hours of the year.


## Continuing bonds, not closure


Members arrive believing the goal is to let go, because that is what they have been told. The work described by Klass, Silverman and Nickman points somewhere else: that an ongoing, changed relationship with the person who died is a normal part of adapting, rather than evidence of being stuck.


That reframe lands hard and well in a group. It gives people permission for the thing they are already doing and hiding.


Questions that open it up:


- "What is one thing from this relationship you still carry?"
- "Is there something you still do because of them?"
- "What would they say about this, if you had to guess?"


Steer away from closure language entirely, including the friendly versions. Adjustment, meaning, remembering, living alongside it. Not moving on.


## Grief support group activities: objects, photos and what members bring


In a grief group people bring things: a photograph, a ring they turn during the session, a voicemail they have not deleted, a jacket.


Let them. A member holding an object is often able to say more, not less. If someone wants to show the group a photograph, that is usually a good session, and you can invite it deliberately: "If you'd like to, bring something of theirs next week. You don't have to explain it."


Two cautions. Keep it optional, loudly, because not everyone has an object or wants one seen. And keep an eye on the clock, because a show-and-tell session will take the whole hour and should be planned as though it will.


If you would rather not build exercises from scratch,[the MentalHappy Resource Library](https://www.mentalhappy.com/resources) has free worksheets and reflection sheets organized by life experience, no account needed.


## When grief may need more than the group


You are not evaluating anyone. You are noticing when what is in front of you is outside what the group was built for.


Things worth a referral conversation: an inability to function that is not easing at all, escalating substance use, severe trauma symptoms, or a member who says the group is the only thing keeping them going.


There is also a clinical picture, prolonged grief disorder, added to the DSM-5-TR in 2022, which a clinician may consider where intense grief persists at least twelve months after the death and is getting in the way of daily life. ICD-11 uses a six month minimum. You are not diagnosing it and should not name it to a member. It is useful only as a reason to say: this is worth talking to someone about, and there is a recognized thing to talk about.


**If a member discloses thoughts of suicide, self-harm, or being in danger, that is not a referral conversation. Give the crisis line, 988 by call or text and 911 for immediate danger, and report it through Support inside the app the same day. The walkthrough is in[When a Group Member Discloses Something Serious](https://www.mentalhappy.com/blog/when-a-member-discloses-something-serious) .**


## Closing the group


In a closed cohort this is the part most often left until it is already happening, and in a grief group that is a particular unkindness: you are ending a relationship with people who came to you because a relationship ended.


1. Name the ending at least three sessions out, then again each week. No surprises.
2. Use the second to last session for what people are taking with them, not for new material.
3. Use the last session to close properly: what changed, what they are still carrying, what they want to do next.
4. Be specific about what happens after. Whether there is another cohort, whether members may stay in touch, whether you will be reachable and in what way.
5. Say the thing out loud: that the group ending does not mean the grief is finished, and that needing support after this is not a failure of the eight weeks.


For an open group, run a smaller version of this whenever a member leaves. An unremarked departure teaches everyone else that people here just disappear, which in a grief group is the exact wrong lesson.


## Between sessions


Ten minutes after each session is worth more than an hour of planning before the next one. Note who spoke and who did not, what the group circled back to, what you cut short, any dates you learned, and anything needing follow-up.


Keep it factual. What was said and what you did, not your theories about what it meant. If anything in it crosses into a safety concern, it goes into an incident report through Support in the app rather than a private note.


## Looking after yourself


Grief groups take something. You are holding several people's worst year at once, week after week, and if you are also grieving something the room will find it.


Decide in advance how many grief sessions a week you can run, whether you need a gap after one, and where you put what you are carrying afterward. The Leaders Lounge exists partly for this.


A facilitator who burns out helps nobody, and members of a grief group are poorly served by another absence.


## Questions about running a grief group


### How should a grief support group session be structured?


Give it a consistent arc: a short welcome, a contained check-in, a brief framing or piece of psychoeducation, the main discussion, a reflection, and a deliberate close. For a 60 minute group that is roughly 5, 10, 7, 23, 7 and 8 minutes. The exact split matters less than protecting the last eight minutes so the session does not end on its hardest moment.


### How do you run a grief support group week to week?


Keep the session shape identical week to week, follow the group rather than your topic plan when the two diverge, and track the dates members bring with them. Expect the account of what happened in early sessions, secondary losses once the group settles, the feelings members are ashamed of in the middle, and identity later. Protect the last eight minutes of every session.


### What topics should a grief support group cover?


Early sessions usually need room for the account of what happened. After that, useful themes include secondary losses, the emotions members feel guilty about, changed family relationships, identity after the loss, difficult days and dates, and what members want to carry forward. Plan themes loosely and follow the group when it goes somewhere else.


### How do I handle a member who compares their loss to someone else's?


Address it as a group norm rather than correcting one person. Say that the group does not rank losses and that nobody needs to qualify their grief before sharing. If one member keeps minimizing their own loss, raise it privately rather than in the room.


### What do I do about anniversaries and holidays in a grief group?


Ask once, early, whether anyone has significant dates coming up, and keep a private note. Leave space in the session before a date without putting the person on the spot. For the holidays, a dedicated session before the season covering what members are dreading and what they are allowed to decline is usually one of the most valuable hours of the year.


### Should a grief group work through the stages of grief?


No. Stage models set members up to believe they are doing grief wrong when anger or sadness returns. A more useful frame is the dual process model, where people move back and forth between confronting the loss and getting on with a changed life. That oscillation is the process.


### How do I end a grief support group well?


Name the ending at least three sessions ahead and repeat it each week. Use the penultimate session for what members are taking with them, and the last one to close deliberately. Be specific about what happens next, and say plainly that the group ending does not mean the grief is finished.


### What if a grieving member seems to need more help than the group can give?


Notice, do not diagnose. Persistent inability to function, escalating substance use or severe trauma symptoms are reasons to have a referral conversation. If a member discloses thoughts of suicide, self-harm or being in danger, give the crisis line, 988 by call or text, and file an incident report through Support in the app the same day.


### What activities work in a grief support group?


The ones with a clear purpose and an easy exit. A two-column exercise on what makes hard days harder and what makes them slightly easier. A question about what members still carry from the relationship. Inviting members to bring an object or photograph, loudly optional, because not everyone has one or wants it seen. Avoid anything that implies grief can be resolved by completing a worksheet.


## Sources
